> **Title**: DNS-Inspired Cryptographic Trust Resolution for Multi-Agent Identity Discovery

# Problem Statement

## Market Perspective

Multi-agent AI is growing fast. Enterprises are deploying autonomous systems that span cloud environments, edge infrastructure, and third-party platforms, and these agents need to work together across organizational lines. They negotiate contracts, share data, and delegate complex tasks without a human in the loop. The problem is that there is no standard way for one agent to discover another agent, verify who it is, or figure out whether it should be trusted with sensitive work. So everyone falls back on brittle, one-off integration patterns that break down at scale.

Here is where the pain really shows up: every new agent-to-agent interaction today requires someone to manually configure endpoints, credentials, and trust assumptions. When your agent ecosystem has a dozen participants, that is annoying but manageable. When it grows to thousands, it is a dead end. Enterprises are stuck choosing between walled garden platforms (which kill interoperability) and open communication with minimal identity checking (which invites impersonation and data leakage). Neither option works for production workloads that touch regulated data or mission critical processes.

The opportunity is basically the same thing DNS did for the early internet, but for agents. A standard protocol for agent identity discovery and trust verification would make cross-organizational agent collaboration actually work at scale. It would be foundational infrastructure for the agentic economy. Whoever defines this protocol first will shape how agent interoperability works for a long time.

## Industry Perspective

The AI industry has converged on multi-agent architectures as the go-to approach for complex task execution. Frameworks like LangGraph, AutoGen, CrewAI, and various proprietary enterprise orchestration platforms all assume agents will discover and interact with other agents on the fly. But the industry has mostly treated agent discovery and trust as application-layer concerns, leaving each framework to cook up its own identity and authorization scheme. Nothing works across frameworks, cloud providers, or organizational boundaries in any standard way.

How do agents identify themselves today? Static API keys. OAuth tokens scoped to platform-level accounts. Simple capability manifests with no cryptographic backing. These mechanisms were designed for human-initiated service calls, not for autonomous agent-to-agent delegation where neither side has a human watching at the time of interaction. The gap gets especially dangerous with trust chains. Say Agent A delegates to Agent B, which sub-delegates to Agent C. There is no way to verify that Agent C is actually authorized by whoever originally set things in motion.

Existing service discovery protocols (DNS, mDNS, service meshes) solve adjacent problems but lack the semantic richness that agent ecosystems need. They resolve network endpoints, sure, but they cannot express agent capabilities, security attestations, governance authority, trust levels, or any of the things that matter when you are deciding whether to delegate a sensitive task to an autonomous system. Similarly, service description formats like OpenAPI and WSDL describe interface contracts for request/response APIs, but they do not capture what matters for autonomous delegation: what an agent is authorized to do, who vouches for it, what trust tier it holds, what data handling policies it enforces, what jurisdictional constraints apply. What the industry needs is a purpose-built resolution protocol that combines DNS-style scalability with public key infrastructure rigor and a capability vocabulary designed specifically for agents.

## Legal & Compliance Perspective

Regulatory frameworks worldwide are expanding quickly to cover autonomous AI systems. The EU AI Act, the US Executive Order on AI, sector-specific regulations in finance, healthcare, and defense: all of them impose requirements around AI system identification, accountability, and auditability. When agents operate across organizational boundaries, figuring out which entity is legally on the hook for an agent's actions becomes a critical compliance question. Without a verifiable identity and trust chain, organizations cannot show regulators that they did their due diligence when selecting and authorizing the agents they interacted with.

Data protection regulations like GDPR and emerging US state privacy laws have strict requirements on data sharing between entities. When an agent delegates a task involving personal data to another agent in a different jurisdiction or organization, both sides need to verify authorization and establish a lawful basis for the data transfer. Current agent architectures provide no standard way to encode data handling policies, jurisdictional constraints, or governance authority into the discovery and handshake process. That creates real compliance risk for any enterprise running cross-boundary agent workflows.

Agentic AI also introduces liability concerns around impersonation and unauthorized delegation that are, as far as we can tell, largely unaddressed. A rogue agent that falsely claims to represent a trusted organization could exfiltrate data, execute unauthorized transactions, or inject bad results into a decision pipeline. Without cryptographically verifiable identity records and trust resolution, organizations have limited ability to detect or prevent these attacks, and limited forensic evidence for incident response or legal proceedings afterward.

## Core Problem

There is no standard, cryptographically verifiable protocol for autonomous AI agents to discover, authenticate, and establish trust with other agents across organizational, platform, and jurisdictional boundaries. Existing service discovery and identity mechanisms lack the semantic richness, trust chain validation, and policy awareness required for secure agent-to-agent delegation. This leaves enterprises exposed to impersonation, unauthorized task execution, and regulatory non-compliance as multi-agent systems scale beyond controlled environments.

---

# Technical Implementation

## Invention Summary

### Core Novelty
We propose the Agent Identity and Trust Resolution Protocol (AITRP), a DNS-inspired resolution layer built specifically for multi-agent systems. AITRP lets agents discover, authenticate, and establish trust relationships before any task delegation or data exchange happens. Unlike traditional service discovery mechanisms that just resolve network endpoints, AITRP resolves cryptographically verifiable identity records that bundle capabilities, trust levels, communication protocols, security attestations, and public keys into a single queryable resource. The protocol supports hierarchical trust chains so agents can validate authorization lineage all the way back to specific organizations, platforms, or governance authorities. This creates a decentralized trust fabric for heterogeneous agent ecosystems.

A key part of what makes AITRP different is the Agent Capability Description Language (ACDL). This is a structured capability vocabulary designed specifically for agent semantics, not API contract description. Service description formats like OpenAPI or WSDL describe HTTP endpoints, request schemas, and response formats for synchronous request/response APIs. ACDL captures properties that matter for autonomous delegation: what domain tasks an agent can perform, what data sensitivity levels it can handle, what jurisdictional constraints govern its operations, what compliance certifications it holds, and what delegation policies it enforces (for example, whether it may sub-delegate to other agents). ACDL uses a hierarchical namespace with versioned capability URIs, so the vocabulary can evolve without breaking existing resolution queries. Agents register capabilities at whatever granularity makes sense, from broad domain categories to fine-grained task types, and querying agents can match at any level in the hierarchy.

### Sequential Inventive Steps
1. **Step 1: Agent Identity Record Registration**: Each agent registers a structured, cryptographically signed identity record with a distributed resolution infrastructure. The record contains the agent's unique identifier, capability manifest expressed in ACDL, supported communication protocols, security attestation proofs, trust tier classification, and one or more public keys. Registration includes validation by the agent's sponsoring authority to prevent unauthorized entries.

2. **Step 2: Trust Resolution Query**: When an agent needs to delegate work or exchange data, it issues a trust resolution query analogous to a DNS lookup. The query retrieves the target agent's signed identity record along with associated policy metadata, capability descriptions, and trust chain certificates. The resolution infrastructure returns results from the nearest authoritative source, supporting caching and TTL semantics for performance. Capability-based queries let agents discover previously unknown agents by specifying required capabilities and minimum trust tiers rather than explicit identifiers.

3. **Step 3: Trust Chain Validation**: The querying agent traverses the trust chain embedded in the resolved identity record, verifying each link from the target agent up through intermediate authorities to a recognized root governance authority. This step confirms that the target agent is authorized by a legitimate organization or platform and that its trust level meets the minimum threshold required for the intended interaction.

4. **Step 4: Secure Channel Establishment and Task Delegation**: After successful trust resolution and chain validation, the agents negotiate a secure communication channel using the public keys and protocol preferences from their respective identity records. Task delegation proceeds with mutual authentication, and all interactions are logged against the resolved identity records for auditability and governance compliance.

### Additional Claims
- **Claim 1**: A capability matching subsystem within the resolution protocol that allows querying agents to discover agents by capability type, trust tier, or organizational affiliation rather than by explicit identifier. This enables dynamic composition of agent workflows based on required skills and authorization levels. The subsystem uses ACDL's hierarchical namespace to support both exact and prefix-based capability matching, so a query for "healthcare.genomics" matches agents registered with "healthcare.genomics.variant_analysis" or "healthcare.genomics.sequence_alignment" unless the query specifies exact match semantics.
- **Claim 2**: A trust revocation and propagation mechanism that allows governance authorities to revoke or downgrade an agent's trust status. Changes propagate through the resolution infrastructure in near real time using signed revocation events that override cached TTLs, making sure that compromised or decommissioned agents are immediately excluded from future task delegations. The mechanism supports both standard revocations (which take effect as cached records expire) and emergency revocations (which carry a TTL override flag that forces immediate cache invalidation across all resolver nodes that have cached the affected record).
- **Claim 3**: A trust anchor bootstrap and rotation protocol that enables new agents and resolver nodes to obtain an authenticated initial set of root trust anchors through a verifiable distribution mechanism. It also supports scheduled anchor rotation with overlap periods to prevent trust disruption during key transitions.

### Value to IBM
AITRP positions IBM at the center of the emerging multi-agent infrastructure market by establishing a foundational protocol layer that every enterprise agent deployment will need. As organizations adopt agentic AI across hybrid cloud environments, standardized identity resolution and trust management becomes a hard requirement. We can integrate AITRP into watsonx, IBM Cloud, and our consulting practice to offer end-to-end agent governance, which differentiates us from competitors who focus on agent capabilities without addressing the trust and security substrate.

The protocol also plays to IBM's existing strengths in enterprise security, identity management, and hybrid cloud orchestration. By owning the trust resolution layer, we create a strategic control point in the agent ecosystem, similar in some ways to how DNS became essential infrastructure for the web. This positions IBM to capture value from every cross-organizational agent interaction, whether agents run on IBM infrastructure or elsewhere. It also aligns with IBM's broader strategy of providing governance and compliance tooling for AI systems operating under regulatory scrutiny.

## Implementation

### Primary Approach
The core implementation is a distributed resolution service built on a hierarchical zone architecture similar to DNS, but designed for agent identity records instead of hostname-to-IP mappings. Each zone corresponds to an organizational or platform boundary and is managed by an authoritative resolver operated by the governing entity. Identity records are stored as signed Protocol Buffer messages. Each one contains the agent's DID (Decentralized Identifier), a capability manifest encoded in ACDL, trust chain certificates in X.509 format, public keys for both authentication and encryption, and metadata about supported interaction protocols.

#### Agent Capability Description Language (ACDL)

ACDL is the structured vocabulary that AITRP uses to describe what an agent can do, what it is authorized to handle, and what constraints govern its operations. It is fundamentally different from service description formats like OpenAPI and WSDL in both scope and purpose:

- **OpenAPI and WSDL** describe API surface area: HTTP methods, URL paths, request/response schemas, authentication schemes, and error codes. They answer the question "how do I call this service?" They are designed for developers integrating with a known API and assume a human will read the spec and write client code.
- **ACDL** describes agent semantics: domain capabilities, data sensitivity authorizations, jurisdictional constraints, compliance attestations, delegation policies, and operational boundaries. It answers the question "can I trust this agent with this task?" ACDL is designed for machine consumption, so autonomous agents can evaluate potential collaborators programmatically with no human involvement.

ACDL capabilities are organized in a hierarchical namespace using dot-separated segments, similar to Java package naming. For example, `finance.risk.credit_scoring` is a descendant of `finance.risk`, which is a descendant of `finance`. Each capability URI is versioned with a `@major.minor` suffix (e.g., `finance.risk.credit_scoring@2.1`), and resolution queries support both exact version matching and compatibility range matching. Major version increments indicate breaking changes to the capability's expected inputs, outputs, or behavioral contract. Minor version increments indicate backward-compatible additions.

Each ACDL capability entry in an identity record includes:
- **Capability URI**: the hierarchical, versioned identifier (e.g., `healthcare.genomics.variant_analysis@1.0`)
- **Data sensitivity level**: the maximum data classification the agent is authorized to process for this capability (public, internal, confidential, restricted)
- **Jurisdictional scope**: a list of jurisdictions where the agent is authorized to operate for this capability, encoded as ISO 3166 country codes
- **Delegation policy**: whether the agent may sub-delegate tasks related to this capability to other agents, and if so, what minimum trust tier the sub-delegate must hold
- **Compliance tags**: references to compliance certifications relevant to this capability (e.g., "HIPAA", "SOC2", "PCI-DSS")

We govern the ACDL namespace through a registration process managed by the root governance authorities in the AITRP hierarchy. New top-level capability domains (e.g., `healthcare`, `finance`, `logistics`) are registered through a governance proposal process. Sub-namespaces can be defined by organizational zone operators for domain-specific extensions. The idea is to balance standardization at the top level with extensibility at the organizational level. This avoids both the rigidity of a fully centralized vocabulary and the fragmentation of an ungoverned namespace.

What this means in practice: when an agent queries the resolver for `healthcare.genomics` with a minimum trust tier of Tier 2 and a data sensitivity level of "confidential", the resolver can evaluate candidate records against all of these constraints and return only agents that are both capable and authorized for the requested task. This kind of policy-aware, semantically rich resolution is just not possible with endpoint-oriented service descriptions.

#### Resolution Process

The resolution process starts when a requesting agent issues a query to its local resolver, specifying either a target agent identifier or a capability-based discovery query. The local resolver checks its cache and, if the record is missing or has expired, forwards the query up the hierarchy to the authoritative zone resolver. The authoritative resolver returns the signed identity record along with the full trust chain. The requesting agent validates the chain using a set of pre-configured root trust anchors, similar to how TLS certificate validation works in web browsers.

Trust chain validation uses a layered model with three tiers. Tier 1 agents are directly attested by a root governance authority and carry the highest trust level. Tier 2 agents are attested by Tier 1 agents or by intermediate authorities that chain back to a root. Tier 3 agents are self-attested and carry the lowest trust level, suitable only for low-sensitivity interactions. Each identity record includes a trust policy document that specifies which tiers and which capability combinations are required for different interaction types.

#### Cross-Zone Trust Chain Traversal

When agents belong to different organizations, each running its own zone resolver under its own zone authority, trust resolution requires traversal across zone boundaries. This cross-zone resolution is fundamental to what makes AITRP useful in multi-organizational deployments. Here is how it works:

Consider two enterprises, Acme Corp and Beacon Labs, each operating its own AITRP zone. Acme's zone authority has signing key `K_acme` and Beacon's has `K_beacon`. Both zone authorities are registered with and attested by a shared root governance authority (say, an industry consortium) with signing key `K_root`. The root authority maintains a registry of all recognized zone authorities and their public keys.

When Acme's procurement agent needs to delegate a compliance verification task to an agent it has never interacted with, the full resolution path goes through these stages:

1. Acme's procurement agent issues a capability discovery query to Acme's local resolver for `compliance.trade_sanctions_screening@1.0` at minimum Tier 2.
2. Acme's local resolver does not have a matching record in its own zone. It forwards the query to the root resolver, which maintains a registry of which zones have registered agents with matching capabilities.
3. The root resolver identifies that Beacon Labs' zone contains a matching agent and returns a referral to Beacon's authoritative zone resolver, along with Beacon's zone authority certificate (signed by `K_root`).
4. Acme's resolver queries Beacon's authoritative zone resolver directly, requesting the identity record for Beacon's compliance agent.
5. Beacon's zone resolver returns the signed identity record for its compliance agent. The record carries two signatures: the issuer signature from Beacon's zone authority (`K_beacon`) and the zone signature from Beacon's zone resolver.
6. Acme's resolver constructs the full trust chain: Beacon's compliance agent is signed by `K_beacon`, which is signed by `K_root`, which is present in Acme's pre-configured root trust anchors. Each signature is verified in sequence.
7. Acme's resolver also verifies the ACDL capability entry in the resolved record, confirming that the compliance agent declares `compliance.trade_sanctions_screening@1.0` with sufficient data sensitivity authorization and jurisdictional coverage.
8. The resolved record, along with the validated trust chain, is cached at Acme's local resolver with the TTL specified in the record, so subsequent queries for the same agent do not require cross-zone traversal until the cache expires.

This cross-zone traversal model mirrors DNS delegation, where a query for `api.beacon-labs.example.com` traverses from the root nameserver to the `example.com` zone to the `beacon-labs.example.com` subdomain. The key difference is that each step in the AITRP traversal also carries cryptographic attestation and rich capability metadata. So the final result is not just a network endpoint but a fully verified identity record with semantic context for the requesting agent's delegation decision.

#### Trust Anchor Bootstrap and Rotation

A critical deployment concern for any PKI-based system is how participating entities get their initial set of root trust anchors and how those anchors are updated over time. We address this through a dedicated bootstrap and rotation protocol.

**Initial Bootstrap.** When a new agent or resolver node joins the AITRP ecosystem, it needs an authenticated set of root trust anchors before it can validate any identity records. We support three bootstrap mechanisms, each suited to different deployment contexts:

- **Organizational provisioning**: In enterprise deployments, the organization's IT governance team provisions trust anchors as part of the agent's deployment configuration, similar to how operating systems ship with pre-installed root CA certificates. The trust anchor bundle is signed by the organization's zone authority, and the agent verifies this signature using a single organizational root key that is embedded at build time or delivered through the organization's existing secure configuration management pipeline (e.g., HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, or Kubernetes Secrets).
- **Consortium enrollment**: When an agent joins a multi-organizational consortium, it submits an enrollment request to the consortium's root governance authority. The enrollment process requires out-of-band identity verification (for example, cryptographic proof of organizational membership or a signed enrollment token issued by the consortium's administrative body). Once verified, the governance authority issues a signed trust anchor bundle containing the root keys for all recognized zone authorities in the consortium.
- **Public resolver discovery**: For agents operating in open ecosystems without a pre-existing organizational relationship, we define a well-known HTTPS endpoint (`.well-known/aitrp-anchors`) hosted by public root governance authorities. The agent retrieves the trust anchor bundle over TLS, using the web PKI as a bootstrap trust layer. The bundle itself is signed by the root authority's key, and the agent verifies this signature against a fingerprint published through multiple independent channels (the authority's website, public key registries, and industry publications) to mitigate single-point-of-compromise risk. This is analogous to how DNSSEC trust anchors are distributed via RFC 7958.

**Anchor Rotation.** Root trust anchors need to be rotated periodically for cryptographic hygiene and to recover from potential key compromise. We handle rotation through an overlap-based transition protocol:

1. The root governance authority generates a new key pair and publishes a signed anchor rotation announcement containing both the current root key and the new root key, along with a transition timeline specifying the activation date and the sunset date for the old key.
2. The announcement is signed by the current root key, so only the legitimate root authority can kick off a rotation.
3. During the overlap period (between activation and sunset), resolvers and agents accept trust chains anchored to either the old or the new root key. Identity records re-signed under the new key are gradually propagated through the resolver hierarchy as records get refreshed.
4. After the sunset date, resolvers remove the old root key from their trust anchor set. Any identity records still signed only under the old key are treated as expired and must be re-registered.
5. If an emergency rotation is required because of suspected key compromise, the governance authority issues an emergency rotation announcement that sets the sunset date to immediate. This announcement is distributed through the same emergency propagation mechanism used for agent revocations, which gets it out fast.

This overlap model makes sure the trust fabric stays continuous during planned rotations and can recover quickly from unplanned key compromise. This is a practical deployment concern that is absent from most academic proposals for agent identity systems, in our experience.

#### Revocation and Propagation Model

Trust revocation is a critical operational concern in any identity infrastructure. We address it through a signed revocation event system that cascades through the resolver hierarchy. When a governance authority revokes an agent's trust status, it generates a signed revocation event containing the target agent's identifier, the revoking authority's signature, a timestamp, and a revocation severity level. There are two severity levels: standard and emergency.

Standard revocations propagate passively. The authoritative zone resolver marks the record as revoked and stops serving it in response to queries. Downstream caching resolvers continue to serve the cached record until its TTL expires, at which point the refresh query returns the revocation notice and the cache entry is purged. Good enough for planned decommissioning or routine credential rotation.

Emergency revocations propagate actively. The authoritative resolver broadcasts a signed revocation event to all peer resolvers and known downstream caching resolvers. Each receiving resolver validates the revocation signature against the revoking authority's known public key, immediately purges the affected record from its cache regardless of remaining TTL, and forwards the revocation event to its own downstream peers. This fan-out propagation model gets compromised agents excluded from the ecosystem within seconds rather than waiting for TTL expiry, which could be minutes or hours. To prevent replay attacks, each revocation event carries a monotonically increasing sequence number and a short validity window; resolvers reject revocation events with sequence numbers lower than the last processed event for a given agent identifier.

#### Threat Model and Resolver Security

The resolution infrastructure itself is a high-value target, so AITRP incorporates specific defenses against attacks on the resolver layer.

**Cache poisoning.** All resolution responses are cryptographically signed by the authoritative zone resolver using its own key pair, analogous to DNSSEC response signing. Caching resolvers validate the authoritative signature before storing any record. A poisoned response that lacks a valid signature is discarded, and the caching resolver flags the upstream source for investigation. Response signatures cover the full record payload including the trust chain, which prevents partial record substitution.

**Zone authority compromise.** If an authoritative zone resolver's signing key is compromised, the parent authority in the hierarchy can issue an emergency revocation for the zone's signing key. This propagates through the same revocation mechanism used for agent identities. On top of that, each zone's signing key is cross-signed by at least one peer zone authority, creating a secondary validation path. Resolvers that detect a mismatch between the zone signature and the cross-signature quarantine all records from the affected zone and escalate to the root authority.

**Denial of service against resolution queries.** The hierarchical caching architecture inherently mitigates denial of service by distributing query load across caching resolvers. For targeted attacks against authoritative resolvers, AITRP supports anycast deployment of zone resolvers (similar to how root DNS servers operate) and rate limiting with priority queuing that favors resolution queries from authenticated agents with valid identity records over anonymous queries.

**Record tampering in transit.** All resolver-to-resolver communication uses mutual TLS with certificate pinning. Identity records are independently verifiable because they carry the issuing authority's signature; even if an intermediary resolver is compromised and tries to serve a modified record, the requesting agent's trust chain validation will detect the invalid signature and reject the record.

```python
import hashlib
import json
import time
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from enum import IntEnum
from typing import Optional

from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import ed25519
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import serialization


class TrustTier(IntEnum):
    SELF_ATTESTED = 3
    INTERMEDIATE = 2
    ROOT_ATTESTED = 1


class RevocationSeverity(IntEnum):
    STANDARD = 1
    EMERGENCY = 2


class DataSensitivity(IntEnum):
    PUBLIC = 1
    INTERNAL = 2
    CONFIDENTIAL = 3
    RESTRICTED = 4


@dataclass
class ACDLCapability:
    """Single capability entry in the Agent Capability Description Language."""
    uri: str  # e.g. "healthcare.genomics.variant_analysis@1.0"
    data_sensitivity: DataSensitivity = DataSensitivity.PUBLIC
    jurisdictions: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)  # ISO 3166 codes
    allows_subdelegation: bool = False
    subdelegation_min_tier: Optional[TrustTier] = None
    compliance_tags: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)

    @property
    def base_uri(self) -> str:
        return self.uri.split("@")[0]

    @property
    def version(self) -> str:
        parts = self.uri.split("@")
        return parts[1] if len(parts) > 1 else "1.0"

    @property
    def major_version(self) -> int:
        return int(self.version.split(".")[0])

    def matches_query(
        self,
        query_uri: str,
        min_sensitivity: Optional[DataSensitivity] = None,
        required_jurisdictions: Optional[list[str]] = None,
        exact_match: bool = False,
    ) -> bool:
        query_base = query_uri.split("@")[0]
        if exact_match:
            if self.base_uri != query_base:
                return False
        else:
            if not self.base_uri.startswith(query_base):
                if self.base_uri != query_base:
                    return False

        query_parts = query_uri.split("@")
        if len(query_parts) > 1:
            query_major = int(query_parts[1].split(".")[0])
            if self.major_version != query_major:
                return False

        if min_sensitivity and self.data_sensitivity < min_sensitivity:
            return False

        if required_jurisdictions:
            if not all(j in self.jurisdictions for j in required_jurisdictions):
                return False

        return True

    def serialize(self) -> dict:
        return {
            "uri": self.uri,
            "data_sensitivity": int(self.data_sensitivity),
            "jurisdictions": sorted(self.jurisdictions),
            "allows_subdelegation": self.allows_subdelegation,
            "subdelegation_min_tier": (
                int(self.subdelegation_min_tier)
                if self.subdelegation_min_tier
                else None
            ),
            "compliance_tags": sorted(self.compliance_tags),
        }

    acdl_capabilities: list[ACDLCapability]
    trust_tier: TrustTier
    public_key_bytes: bytes
    supported_protocols: list[str]
    issuer_id: str
    zone_id: str = ""
    issued_at: float = field(default_factory=time.time)
    ttl_seconds: int = 3600
    trust_chain: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)

        min_sensitivity: Optional[DataSensitivity] = None,
        required_jurisdictions: Optional[list[str]] = None,

            for c in self.acdl_capabilities

            "trust_tier": int(self.trust_tier),
            "public_key": self.public_key_bytes.hex(),
            "supported_protocols": sorted(self.supported_protocols),
            "issuer_id": self.issuer_id,
            "zone_id": self.zone_id,
            "issued_at": self.issued_at,
            "ttl_seconds": self.ttl_seconds,
            "trust_chain": self.trust_chain,
        }
        return json.dumps(payload, sort_keys=True).encode("utf-8")

class TrustResolver:
    def __init__(
        self,
        root_trust_anchors: dict[str, ed25519.Ed25519PublicKey],
        zone_id: str = "default",
        zone_signing_key: Optional[ed25519.Ed25519PrivateKey] = None,
    ):
        self._cache: dict[str, AgentIdentityRecord] = {}
        self._root_anchors = root_trust_anchors
        self._zone_records: dict[str, AgentIdentityRecord] = {}
        self._zone_id = zone_id
        self._zone_signing_key = zone_signing_key
        self._revocation_log: dict[str, RevocationEvent] = {}
        self._peer_resolvers: list["TrustResolver"] = []
        self._upstream_resolvers: list["TrustResolver"] = []
        self._last_revocation_seq: dict[str, int] = {}

    def add_peer_resolver(self, peer: "TrustResolver") -> None:
        if peer not in self._peer_resolvers:
            self._peer_resolvers.append(peer)

    def add_upstream_resolver(self, upstream: "TrustResolver") -> None:
        if upstream not in self._upstream_resolvers:
            self._upstream_resolvers.append(upstream)

    def bootstrap_trust_anchors(
        self,
        bundle: TrustAnchorBundle,
        bootstrap_key: ed25519.Ed25519PublicKey,
    ) -> bool:
        if bundle.signature is None:
            return False
        try:
            bootstrap_key.verify(
                bundle.signature, bundle.serialize_for_signing()
            )
        except Exception:
            return False
        if bundle.expires_at > 0 and time.time() > bundle.expires_at:
            return False
        for authority_id, key_bytes in bundle.anchors.items():
            self._root_anchors[authority_id] = (
                ed25519.Ed25519PublicKey.from_public_bytes(key_bytes)
            )
        return True

    def register_identity(
        self,
        record: AgentIdentityRecord,
        issuer_private_key: ed25519.Ed25519PrivateKey,
    ) -> AgentIdentityRecord:
        record.zone_id = self._zone_id
        payload = record.serialize_for_signing()
        record.signature = issuer_private_key.sign(payload)
        if self._zone_signing_key:
            record.zone_signature = self._zone_signing_key.sign(payload)
        self._zone_records[record.agent_id] = record
        return record

    def resolve(self, agent_id: str) -> Optional[AgentIdentityRecord]:
        if agent_id in self._revocation_log:
            return None

        cached = self._cache.get(agent_id)
        if cached and not cached.is_expired():
            return cached

        record = self._zone_records.get(agent_id)
        if record is not None:
            if record.is_expired():
                self._zone_records.pop(agent_id, None)
                self._cache.pop(agent_id, None)
                return None
            self._cache[agent_id] = record
            return record

        for upstream in self._upstream_resolvers:
            record = upstream.resolve(agent_id)
            if record is not None:
                self._cache[agent_id] = record
                return record

        return None

    def resolve_by_capability(
        self,
        capability_uri: str,
        min_trust_tier: TrustTier = TrustTier.SELF_ATTESTED,
        min_sensitivity: Optional[DataSensitivity] = None,
        required_jurisdictions: Optional[list[str]] = None,
    ) -> list[AgentIdentityRecord]:
        results = []
        all_records = dict(self._zone_records)
        for upstream in self._upstream_resolvers:
            for rec in upstream.resolve_by_capability(
                capability_uri, min_trust_tier, min_sensitivity,
                required_jurisdictions,
            ):
                if rec.agent_id not in all_records:
                    all_records[rec.agent_id] = rec

        for record in all_records.values():
            if record.is_expired():
                continue
            if record.agent_id in self._revocation_log:
                continue
            if record.trust_tier > min_trust_tier:
                continue
            if record.has_capability(
                capability_uri, min_sensitivity, required_jurisdictions
            ):
                results.append(record)
        return sorted(results, key=lambda r: r.trust_tier)

    def validate_trust_chain(self, record: AgentIdentityRecord) -> bool:
        if record.signature is None:
            return False

        if record.agent_id in self._revocation_log:
            return False

        payload = record.serialize_for_signing()

        if record.issuer_id in self._root_anchors:
            try:
                self._root_anchors[record.issuer_id].verify(
                    record.signature, payload
                )
                return True
            except Exception:
                return False

        issuer_record = self.resolve(record.issuer_id)
        if issuer_record is None:
            return False

        if not self.validate_trust_chain(issuer_record):
            return False

        try:
            issuer_public_key = ed25519.Ed25519PublicKey.from_public_bytes(
                issuer_record.public_key_bytes
            )
            issuer_public_key.verify(record.signature, payload)
            return True
        except Exception:
            return False

    def revoke(
        self,
        agent_id: str,
        authority_id: str,
        authority_key: ed25519.Ed25519PrivateKey,
        severity: RevocationSeverity = RevocationSeverity.STANDARD,
    ) -> RevocationEvent:
        last_seq = self._last_revocation_seq.get(agent_id, 0)
        new_seq = last_seq + 1

        event = RevocationEvent(
            target_agent_id=agent_id,
            revoking_authority_id=authority_id,
            severity=severity,
            sequence_number=new_seq,
        )
        event.signature = authority_key.sign(event.serialize_for_signing())

        self._apply_revocation(event)

        if severity == RevocationSeverity.EMERGENCY:
            self._propagate_emergency_revocation(event)

        return event

    def _apply_revocation(self, event: RevocationEvent) -> bool:
        last_seq = self._last_revocation_seq.get(event.target_agent_id, 0)
        if event.sequence_number <= last_seq:
            return False
        if not event.is_valid():
            return False

        authority_key = self._root_anchors.get(event.revoking_authority_id)
        if authority_key is None:
            issuer_record = self._zone_records.get(event.revoking_authority_id)
            if issuer_record is None:
                return False
            try:
                authority_key = ed25519.Ed25519PublicKey.from_public_bytes(
                    issuer_record.public_key_bytes
                )
            except Exception:
                return False

        try:
            authority_key.verify(
                event.signature, event.serialize_for_signing()
            )
        except Exception:
            return False

        self._revocation_log[event.target_agent_id] = event
        self._last_revocation_seq[event.target_agent_id] = (
            event.sequence_number
        )
        self._zone_records.pop(event.target_agent_id, None)
        self._cache.pop(event.target_agent_id, None)
        return True

    def _propagate_emergency_revocation(self, event: RevocationEvent) -> None:
        for peer in self._peer_resolvers:
            peer.receive_revocation_event(event)

    def receive_revocation_event(self, event: RevocationEvent) -> bool:
        if event.severity != RevocationSeverity.EMERGENCY:
            return False
        applied = self._apply_revocation(event)
        if applied:
            for peer in self._peer_resolvers:
                peer.receive_revocation_event(event)
        return applied


class AgentHandshake:
    def __init__(self, resolver: TrustResolver):
        self._resolver = resolver

    def initiate(
        self,
        requesting_agent: AgentIdentityRecord,
        target_agent_id: str,
        required_capability: str,
        min_trust_tier: TrustTier = TrustTier.INTERMEDIATE,
        min_sensitivity: Optional[DataSensitivity] = None,
        required_jurisdictions: Optional[list[str]] = None,
    ) -> dict:
        target_record = self._resolver.resolve(target_agent_id)
        if target_record is None:
            return {"status": "failed", "reason": "agent_not_found"}

        if not target_record.has_capability(
            required_capability, min_sensitivity, required_jurisdictions
        ):
            return {"status": "failed", "reason": "capability_mismatch"}

        if target_record.trust_tier > min_trust_tier:
            return {"status": "failed", "reason": "insufficient_trust_tier"}

        if not self._resolver.validate_trust_chain(target_record):
            return {"status": "failed", "reason": "trust_chain_invalid"}

        common_protocols = set(requesting_agent.supported_protocols) & set(
            target_record.supported_protocols
        )
        if not common_protocols:
            return {"status": "failed", "reason": "no_common_protocol"}

        session_id = hashlib.sha256(
            f"{requesting_agent.agent_id}:{target_agent_id}:{time.time()}".encode()
        ).hexdigest()[:16]

        return {
            "status": "established",
            "session_id": session_id,
            "negotiated_protocol": sorted(common_protocols)[0],
            "target_trust_tier": int(target_record.trust_tier),
            "target_capabilities": [
                c.serialize() for c in target_record.acdl_capabilities
            ],
            "target_zone": target_record.zone_id,
        }

    def discover_and_initiate(
        self,
        requesting_agent: AgentIdentityRecord,
        required_capability: str,
        min_trust_tier: TrustTier = TrustTier.INTERMEDIATE,
        min_sensitivity: Optional[DataSensitivity] = None,
        required_jurisdictions: Optional[list[str]] = None,
    ) -> dict:
        candidates = self._resolver.resolve_by_capability(
            required_capability, min_trust_tier, min_sensitivity,
            required_jurisdictions,
        )
        if not candidates:
            return {"status": "failed", "reason": "no_capable_agents_found"}

        for candidate in candidates:
            if not self._resolver.validate_trust_chain(candidate):
                continue

            common_protocols = set(requesting_agent.supported_protocols) & set(
                candidate.supported_protocols
            )
            if not common_protocols:
                continue

            session_id = hashlib.sha256(
                f"{requesting_agent.agent_id}:{candidate.agent_id}:{time.time()}".encode()
            ).hexdigest()[:16]

            return {
                "status": "established",
                "session_id": session_id,
                "discovered_agent_id": candidate.agent_id,
                "negotiated_protocol": sorted(common_protocols)[0],
                "target_trust_tier": int(candidate.trust_tier),
                "target_capabilities": [
                    c.serialize() for c in candidate.acdl_capabilities
                ],
                "target_zone": candidate.zone_id,
            }

        return {
            "status": "failed",
            "reason": "no_valid_agents_after_verification",
        }
```

The `ACDLCapability` class represents a single entry in the Agent Capability Description Language. Each capability carries a versioned hierarchical URI, a data sensitivity authorization level, a list of jurisdictional scopes, delegation policy flags, and compliance certification tags. The `matches_query` method supports both exact matching and prefix-based hierarchical matching: a query for `healthcare.genomics` will match agents registered with `healthcare.genomics.variant_analysis@1.0`, which enables discovery at any level of the capability hierarchy. Version matching uses major version compatibility semantics, so a query for `@2` matches `@2.0` and `@2.3` but not `@1.0` or `@3.0`.

`AgentIdentityRecord` holds the full identity payload for a single agent, using `acdl_capabilities` instead of flat string capability lists. The `has_capability` method evaluates a query against all registered capabilities, checking not just the capability URI but also data sensitivity authorization and jurisdictional coverage. The `zone_id` field identifies which organizational zone the agent belongs to, which enables cross-zone resolution tracking. The `zone_signature` field carries the authoritative zone resolver's signature over the record so downstream caching resolvers can verify record authenticity independently of the issuing authority's signature.

`TrustAnchorBundle` represents a signed collection of root trust anchors used for bootstrap and rotation. The `supersedes_bundle_hash` field creates an auditable chain of anchor updates, letting resolvers verify that a rotation announcement was actually issued by the authority that controlled the previous anchor set.

`RevocationEvent` represents a signed revocation notification carrying the target agent's identifier, the revoking authority's identity, a severity level, and a monotonically increasing sequence number. The sequence number prevents replay attacks: resolvers reject any revocation event with a sequence number at or below the last processed event for a given agent. The validity window makes sure that stale revocation events cannot be replayed after their intended propagation period has elapsed.

`TrustResolver` is the core resolution infrastructure. It maintains authoritative zone records, a local cache with TTL expiration, a revocation log, a list of peer resolvers for emergency propagation, and a list of upstream resolvers for cross-zone query forwarding. The `resolve` method basically mirrors DNS lookup behavior by checking the revocation log first, then the local cache, then the authoritative store, and finally upstream resolvers for records in other zones. `resolve_by_capability` enables discovery queries where the requesting agent specifies what it needs rather than who it needs, returning matching agents sorted by trust tier while filtering on data sensitivity, jurisdictional constraints, and revocation status. `validate_trust_chain` recursively walks the issuer chain, verifying signatures at each level until it reaches a recognized root trust anchor, and rejects any agent that appears in the revocation log. The `bootstrap_trust_anchors` method lets a new resolver load its initial root anchors from a signed bundle, with signature verification against a known bootstrap key.

The `revoke` method supports two severity levels. Standard revocations remove the record from the authoritative store; cached copies at downstream resolvers expire naturally via TTL. Emergency revocations trigger active propagation: `_propagate_emergency_revocation` pushes the signed revocation event to all peer resolvers, each of which validates the event signature, purges the affected record immediately regardless of remaining TTL, and forwards the event to its own peers. This fan-out model means a compromised agent gets excluded from the ecosystem within seconds.

`AgentHandshake` orchestrates the full pre-communication workflow. The `initiate` method covers the case where the requesting agent already knows the target's identifier: resolution, ACDL capability matching (including data sensitivity and jurisdictional checks), trust tier enforcement, trust chain validation, and protocol negotiation. `discover_and_initiate` handles the open discovery case where the requesting agent specifies only a required capability, minimum trust tier, and optional policy constraints. It retrieves all matching candidates across local and upstream zones, iterates through them in trust tier order, validates each candidate's trust chain, checks protocol compatibility, and establishes a session with the first agent that passes all checks. This method is the core primitive for open ecosystem composition; it lets agents discover and collaborate with previously unknown agents across organizational boundaries without any prior manual configuration.

### Alternative Approaches

#### Alternative 1: Blockchain Anchored Identity Registry
Instead of a hierarchical resolver architecture, we could anchor agent identity records to a permissioned blockchain where each registration, update, and revocation is recorded as an immutable transaction. Trust chain validation would become a matter of traversing on-chain attestation transactions rather than querying a resolver hierarchy. This gives you stronger tamper resistance and eliminates the need for a centralized authoritative zone operator, but it introduces latency and throughput limitations that make it better suited for infrequent registration and revocation events rather than high-frequency resolution queries. A hybrid model could use the blockchain for registration and revocation while serving resolution queries from an off-chain cache layer synchronized with the ledger.

#### Alternative 2: Federated Web of Trust Model
Rather than relying on hierarchical trust chains rooted in governance authorities, agents could establish trust through a federated web of trust model where mutual attestations between agents accumulate into a trust graph. An agent's effective trust score would be computed by analyzing the graph structure, considering factors like the number of attestations, the trust scores of attesting agents, and how recent those attestations are. This approach works better for decentralized ecosystems where no single governance authority exists, like open research collaborations or cross-industry data sharing consortia. The tradeoff is that trust computation becomes probabilistic rather than deterministic, requiring threshold policies that define minimum graph connectivity for different interaction types.

## Embodiments

### Embodiment 1: Enterprise Hybrid Cloud Agent Orchestration
A multinational financial services company deploys specialized AI agents across IBM Cloud for risk modeling, AWS for market data ingestion, and on-premises infrastructure for regulatory compliance checking. Each agent registers its identity record with the AITRP resolver operated by the company's IT governance team, which serves as the root trust anchor. When the risk modeling agent on IBM Cloud needs to delegate a compliance check, it issues a trust resolution query for agents with the `regulatory.compliance_audit@1.0` capability at Trust Tier 1, specifying a minimum data sensitivity of CONFIDENTIAL and jurisdictional scope of "US". The resolver returns the on-premises compliance agent's signed identity record, including its ACDL capability entry confirming authorization for confidential data in US jurisdiction. The risk modeling agent validates the trust chain back to the company's root authority, confirms protocol compatibility (both support gRPC with mTLS), and establishes a secure session. If the compliance agent's certificate is later revoked due to a security incident, the governance team issues an emergency revocation event. The signed revocation propagates from the authoritative zone resolver to all caching resolvers across the company's hybrid infrastructure within seconds, overriding cached TTLs. Subsequent resolution queries return no valid result, immediately cutting off the compromised agent from the ecosystem. The revocation event's sequence number and validity window prevent any replay attempt from re-introducing the compromised identity.

### Embodiment 2: Cross-Organization Agent Collaboration with Full Cross-Zone Traversal
Two enterprises, a pharmaceutical company (PharmaCo) and a clinical research organization (CRO Labs), have no pre-existing technical integration but are both members of a healthcare industry consortium that operates a shared AITRP root governance authority.

PharmaCo operates its own AITRP zone (`zone:pharmaco`) with zone authority key `K_pharmaco`, attested by the consortium root. CRO Labs operates zone `zone:crolabs` with zone authority key `K_crolabs`, also attested by the consortium root. Each organization has its agents registered under its own zone namespace.

PharmaCo's drug interaction analysis agent runs into a situation: it needs a genomic variant annotation capability that no PharmaCo agent provides. The agent issues a capability discovery query to PharmaCo's local resolver for `healthcare.genomics.variant_analysis@1.0` at minimum Trust Tier 2, with data sensitivity CONFIDENTIAL and jurisdictional scope `["US", "EU"]`, plus a compliance tag filter for "HIPAA".

PharmaCo's local resolver finds no matching record in its own zone. It forwards the query to the consortium's root resolver, which maintains a capability index across all member zones. The root resolver identifies that CRO Labs' zone contains a matching agent and returns a referral to CRO Labs' authoritative zone resolver, along with CRO Labs' zone authority certificate signed by the consortium root key.

PharmaCo's resolver queries CRO Labs' zone resolver, which returns the identity record for CRO Labs' genomic analysis agent. The record includes ACDL capabilities declaring `healthcare.genomics.variant_analysis@1.2` with data sensitivity CONFIDENTIAL, jurisdictions `["US", "EU", "GB"]`, compliance tags `["HIPAA", "GDPR"]`, and a delegation policy permitting sub-delegation only to Tier 1 agents. The record carries the issuer signature from `K_crolabs` and the zone signature from CRO Labs' zone resolver.

PharmaCo's resolver constructs and validates the trust chain: CRO Labs' genomic agent, signed by `K_crolabs`, which is signed by `K_root`, which is present in PharmaCo's configured root trust anchors. The ACDL capability entry is evaluated against the query constraints: version 1.2 satisfies the major version 1 compatibility requirement, CONFIDENTIAL data sensitivity meets the threshold, US and EU jurisdictional coverage is confirmed, and HIPAA compliance is present.

PharmaCo's drug interaction agent gets the fully validated record and initiates a handshake. Both agents support gRPC with mTLS. A session is established, and the genomic analysis task proceeds with mutual authentication. The identity record and trust chain validation provide PharmaCo with auditable evidence that CRO Labs' agent was authorized by a recognized governance authority, met the required compliance standards, and was verified through a cryptographic chain of trust. All of this happened without any prior manual configuration, partnership API key exchange, or direct communication between the two organizations' IT teams.

This embodiment demonstrates the full cross-zone traversal path: local zone lookup, root referral, cross-zone authoritative query, multi-hop trust chain validation, and ACDL-based policy matching. These are the mechanics that distinguish AITRP from single-organization agent management solutions.

### Embodiment 3: Open Ecosystem Capability Discovery via Public Resolver with Trust Anchor Bootstrap
A mid-sized logistics company is deploying its first AITRP-capable agent and has no pre-existing relationship with any AITRP governance authority. The company's DevOps team bootstraps the agent's trust configuration by retrieving a trust anchor bundle from a public root governance authority's well-known HTTPS endpoint (`.well-known/aitrp-anchors`). The bundle is signed by the root authority's key, and the DevOps team verifies the key fingerprint against the authority's published fingerprint in its official documentation and two independent industry registry listings. The agent's resolver loads the verified bundle using the `bootstrap_trust_anchors` method, establishing its initial root of trust.

The logistics agent needs to optimize supply chain routing and hits a new wrinkle: a recent trade regulation requires real-time sanctions screening for shipments transiting certain jurisdictions. The company has no existing relationship with any sanctions screening provider, and none of its internal agents have this capability. The logistics agent queries the AITRP public resolver (a globally accessible resolver tier, analogous to public DNS) with a capability discovery request specifying `compliance.trade_sanctions_screening@1.0`, a minimum trust tier of Tier 2, a data sensitivity of INTERNAL, and jurisdictional scope of `["SG", "MY", "TH"]` (Southeast Asian transit routes).

The public resolver returns identity records for three agents operated by different compliance service providers, each registered under its own organizational zone and attested by recognized industry governance authorities.

The logistics agent evaluates the candidates programmatically. It validates each candidate's trust chain back to a governance authority present in its bootstrapped root trust anchors. One candidate's chain terminates at an unrecognized authority, so it gets discarded. Of the remaining two, the logistics agent checks ACDL capability metadata: one agent's `compliance.trade_sanctions_screening@1.0` entry declares jurisdictional coverage for `["US", "EU"]` only, which does not satisfy the required Southeast Asian jurisdictions. That candidate is excluded by the ACDL jurisdictional filter. The surviving agent declares jurisdictional coverage for `["SG", "MY", "TH", "VN", "ID"]`, holds a compliance tag for "OFAC", supports gRPC with mTLS, and is attested by a Tier 1 financial compliance governance authority.

The logistics agent initiates a handshake using `discover_and_initiate`, establishing a session without any prior manual configuration, partnership agreement, or API key exchange between the two organizations. The sanctions screening agent's identity record, including its ACDL capability manifest with jurisdictional scope and compliance attestations, gives the logistics company auditable evidence of due diligence for regulatory purposes.

Six months later, the public root governance authority rotates its root signing key. The authority publishes a signed anchor rotation announcement containing both the current and new root keys, with a 90-day overlap period. The logistics agent's resolver receives the announcement, verifies it against the current root key, and adds the new key to its trust anchor set. During the overlap period, it accepts trust chains anchored to either key. After the overlap period expires, the old key is removed. The rotation completes with no interruption to the agent's ongoing resolution queries.

If the sanctions screening provider is later found to be compromised, the governance authority that attested it issues an emergency revocation that propagates across the public resolver infrastructure. This automatically excludes it from future discovery results for all querying agents.

This embodiment demonstrates AITRP operating at internet scale in a fully open ecosystem, covering the full lifecycle from initial trust anchor bootstrap through capability-based cross-zone discovery to anchor rotation. Agents discover previously unknown counterparts purely through ACDL capability queries without requiring pre-established organizational relationships, shared consortium membership, or platform co-tenancy.

The Agent Identity and Trust Resolution Protocol (AITRP) introduces a DNS-inspired resolution layer purpose built for multi-agent systems, enabling agents to discover, authenticate, and establish trust relationships before any task delegation or data exchange occurs. Unlike traditional service discovery mechanisms that focus on network endpoints, AITRP resolves cryptographically verifiable identity records that bundle capabilities, trust levels, communication protocols, security attestations, and public keys into a single queryable resource. The protocol supports hierarchical trust chains that allow agents to validate authorization lineage back to specific organizations, platforms, or governance authorities, creating a decentralized trust fabric for heterogeneous agent ecosystems.

A key element of AITRP's novelty is its Agent Capability Description Language (ACDL), a structured capability vocabulary designed specifically for agent semantics rather than API contract description. Unlike service description formats such as OpenAPI or WSDL, which describe HTTP endpoints, request schemas, and response formats for synchronous request/response APIs, ACDL captures the properties that matter for autonomous delegation: what domain tasks an agent can perform, what data sensitivity levels it is authorized to handle, what jurisdictional constraints govern its operations, what compliance certifications it holds, and what delegation policies it enforces (for example, whether it may sub-delegate to other agents). ACDL uses a hierarchical namespace with versioned capability URIs, allowing the vocabulary to evolve without breaking existing resolution queries. Agents can register capabilities at any granularity, from broad domain categories to fine-grained task types, and querying agents can match at any level in the hierarchy.

## Implementation

### Primary Approach
The primary implementation centers on a distributed resolution service built on a hierarchical zone architecture similar to DNS, but designed for agent identity records rather than hostname to IP mappings. Each zone corresponds to an organizational or platform boundary and is managed by an authoritative resolver operated by the governing entity. Identity records are stored as signed Protocol Buffer messages, each containing the agent's DID (Decentralized Identifier), a capability manifest encoded in ACDL, trust chain certificates in X.509 format, public keys for both authentication and encryption, and metadata about supported interaction protocols.

#### Agent Capability Description Language (ACDL)

ACDL is the structured vocabulary that AITRP uses to describe what an agent can do, what it is authorized to handle, and what constraints govern its operations. It differs fundamentally from service description formats like OpenAPI and WSDL in both scope and purpose:

- **OpenAPI and WSDL** describe API surface area: HTTP methods, URL paths, request/response schemas, authentication schemes, and error codes. They answer the question "how do I call this service?" They are designed for developers integrating with a known API and assume a human will read the specification and write client code.
- **ACDL** describes agent semantics: domain capabilities, data sensitivity authorizations, jurisdictional constraints, compliance attestations, delegation policies, and operational boundaries. It answers the question "can I trust this agent with this task?" ACDL is designed for machine consumption, enabling autonomous agents to evaluate potential collaborators programmatically without human involvement.

ACDL capabilities are organized in a hierarchical namespace using dot-separated segments, similar to Java package naming. For example, `finance.risk.credit_scoring` is a descendant of `finance.risk`, which is a descendant of `finance`. Each capability URI is versioned using a `@major.minor` suffix (e.g., `finance.risk.credit_scoring@2.1`), with resolution queries supporting both exact version matching and compatibility range matching. Major version increments indicate breaking changes to the capability's expected inputs, outputs, or behavioral contract. Minor version increments indicate backward-compatible additions.

Each ACDL capability entry in an identity record includes:
- **Capability URI**: the hierarchical, versioned identifier (e.g., `healthcare.genomics.variant_analysis@1.0`)
- **Data sensitivity level**: the maximum data classification the agent is authorized to process for this capability (public, internal, confidential, restricted)
- **Jurisdictional scope**: a list of jurisdictions where the agent is authorized to operate for this capability, encoded as ISO 3166 country codes
- **Delegation policy**: whether the agent may sub-delegate tasks related to this capability to other agents, and if so, what minimum trust tier the sub-delegate must hold
- **Compliance tags**: references to compliance certifications relevant to this capability (e.g., "HIPAA", "SOC2", "PCI-DSS")

The ACDL namespace is governed through a registration process managed by the root governance authorities in the AITRP hierarchy. New top level capability domains (e.g., `healthcare`, `finance`, `logistics`) are registered through a governance proposal process. Sub-namespaces can be defined by organizational zone operators for domain-specific extensions. This approach balances standardization at the top level with extensibility at the organizational level, avoiding both the rigidity of a fully centralized vocabulary and the fragmentation of an ungoverned namespace.

This design means that when an agent queries the resolver for `healthcare.genomics` with a minimum trust tier of Tier 2 and a data sensitivity level of "confidential", the resolver can evaluate candidate records against all of these constraints, returning only agents that are both capable and authorized for the requested task. This kind of policy-aware, semantically rich resolution is impossible with endpoint-oriented service descriptions.

#### Resolution Process

The resolution process begins when a requesting agent issues a query to its local resolver, specifying either a target agent identifier or a capability based discovery query. The local resolver checks its cache and, if the record is not present or has expired, forwards the query up the hierarchy to the authoritative zone resolver. The authoritative resolver returns the signed identity record along with the full trust chain. The requesting agent validates the chain using a set of pre-configured root trust anchors, similar to how TLS certificate validation works in web browsers.

Trust chain validation uses a layered model with three tiers. Tier 1 agents are directly attested by a root governance authority and carry the highest trust level. Tier 2 agents are attested by Tier 1 agents or by intermediate authorities that chain back to a root. Tier 3 agents are self-attested and carry the lowest trust level, suitable only for low sensitivity interactions. Each identity record includes a trust policy document that specifies which tiers and which capability combinations are required for different interaction types.

#### Cross-Zone Trust Chain Traversal

When agents belong to different organizations, each operating its own zone resolver under its own zone authority, trust resolution requires traversal across zone boundaries. This cross-zone resolution is fundamental to AITRP's value in multi-organizational deployments and works as follows:

Consider two enterprises, Acme Corp and Beacon Labs, each operating its own AITRP zone. Acme's zone authority has signing key `K_acme` and Beacon's has `K_beacon`. Both zone authorities are registered with and attested by a shared root governance authority (for example, an industry consortium) with signing key `K_root`. The root authority maintains a registry of all recognized zone authorities and their public keys.

When Acme's procurement agent needs to delegate a compliance verification task to an agent it has never interacted with, the full resolution path proceeds through these stages:

1. Acme's procurement agent issues a capability discovery query to Acme's local resolver for `compliance.trade_sanctions_screening@1.0` at minimum Tier 2.
2. Acme's local resolver does not have a matching record in its own zone. It forwards the query to the root resolver, which maintains a registry of which zones have registered agents with matching capabilities.
3. The root resolver identifies that Beacon Labs' zone contains a matching agent and returns a referral to Beacon's authoritative zone resolver, along with Beacon's zone authority certificate (signed by `K_root`).
4. Acme's resolver queries Beacon's authoritative zone resolver directly, requesting the identity record for Beacon's compliance agent.
5. Beacon's zone resolver returns the signed identity record for its compliance agent. The record carries two signatures: the issuer signature from Beacon's zone authority (`K_beacon`) and the zone signature from Beacon's zone resolver.
6. Acme's resolver constructs the full trust chain: Beacon's compliance agent is signed by `K_beacon`, which is signed by `K_root`, which is present in Acme's pre-configured root trust anchors. Each signature is verified in sequence.
7. Acme's resolver also verifies the ACDL capability entry in the resolved record, confirming that the compliance agent declares `compliance.trade_sanctions_screening@1.0` with sufficient data sensitivity authorization and jurisdictional coverage.
8. The resolved record, along with the validated trust chain, is cached at Acme's local resolver with the TTL specified in the record, so subsequent queries for the same agent do not require cross-zone traversal until the cache expires.

This cross-zone traversal model mirrors DNS delegation, where a query for `api.beacon-labs.example.com` traverses from the root nameserver to the `example.com` zone to the `beacon-labs.example.com` subdomain. The key difference is that each step in the AITRP traversal also carries cryptographic attestation and rich capability metadata, so the final result is not just a network endpoint but a fully verified identity record with semantic context for the requesting agent's delegation decision.

#### Trust Anchor Bootstrap and Rotation

A critical deployment concern for any PKI-based system is how participating entities obtain their initial set of root trust anchors and how those anchors are updated over time. AITRP addresses this through a dedicated bootstrap and rotation protocol.

**Initial Bootstrap.** When a new agent or resolver node joins the AITRP ecosystem, it must obtain an authenticated set of root trust anchors before it can validate any identity records. AITRP supports three bootstrap mechanisms, each suited to different deployment contexts:

- **Organizational provisioning**: In enterprise deployments, the organization's IT governance team provisions trust anchors as part of the agent's deployment configuration, similar to how operating systems ship with a pre-installed set of root CA certificates. The trust anchor bundle is signed by the organization's zone authority, and the agent verifies this signature using a single organizational root key that is embedded at build time or delivered through the organization's existing secure configuration management pipeline (e.g., HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, or Kubernetes Secrets).
- **Consortium enrollment**: When an agent joins a multi-organizational consortium, it submits an enrollment request to the consortium's root governance authority. The enrollment process requires out-of-band identity verification (for example, cryptographic proof of organizational membership or a signed enrollment token issued by the consortium's administrative body). Upon verification, the governance authority issues a signed trust anchor bundle containing the root keys for all recognized zone authorities in the consortium.
- **Public resolver discovery**: For agents operating in open ecosystems without a pre-existing organizational relationship, AITRP defines a well-known HTTPS endpoint (`.well-known/aitrp-anchors`) hosted by public root governance authorities. The agent retrieves the trust anchor bundle over TLS, using the web PKI as a bootstrap trust layer. The bundle itself is signed by the root authority's key, and the agent verifies this signature against a fingerprint published through multiple independent channels (the authority's website, public key registries, and industry publications) to mitigate single-point-of-compromise risk. This approach is analogous to how DNSSEC trust anchors are distributed via RFC 7958.

**Anchor Rotation.** Root trust anchors must be rotated periodically to maintain cryptographic hygiene and to recover from potential key compromise. AITRP handles rotation through an overlap-based transition protocol:

1. The root governance authority generates a new key pair and publishes a signed anchor rotation announcement containing both the current root key and the new root key, along with a transition timeline specifying the activation date and the sunset date for the old key.
2. The announcement is signed by the current root key, ensuring that only the legitimate root authority can initiate a rotation.
3. During the overlap period (between activation and sunset), resolvers and agents accept trust chains anchored to either the old or the new root key. Identity records re-signed under the new key are gradually propagated through the resolver hierarchy as records are refreshed.
4. After the sunset date, resolvers remove the old root key from their trust anchor set. Any identity records still signed only under the old key are treated as expired and must be re-registered.
5. If an emergency rotation is required due to suspected key compromise, the governance authority issues an emergency rotation announcement that sets the sunset date to immediate. This announcement is distributed through the same emergency propagation mechanism used for agent revocations, ensuring rapid dissemination.

This overlap model ensures that the trust fabric remains continuous during planned rotations and can recover rapidly from unplanned key compromise, addressing a practical deployment concern that is absent from most academic proposals for agent identity systems.

#### Revocation and Propagation Model

Trust revocation is a critical operational concern in any identity infrastructure, and AITRP addresses it through a signed revocation event system that cascades through the resolver hierarchy. When a governance authority revokes an agent's trust status, it generates a signed revocation event containing the target agent's identifier, the revoking authority's signature, a timestamp, and a revocation severity level. Two severity levels exist: standard and emergency.

Standard revocations propagate passively. The authoritative zone resolver marks the record as revoked and stops serving it in response to queries. Downstream caching resolvers continue to serve the cached record until its TTL expires, at which point the refresh query returns the revocation notice and the cache entry is purged. This approach is suitable for planned decommissioning or routine credential rotation.

Emergency revocations propagate actively. The authoritative resolver broadcasts a signed revocation event to all peer resolvers and known downstream caching resolvers. Each receiving resolver validates the revocation signature against the revoking authority's known public key, immediately purges the affected record from its cache regardless of remaining TTL, and forwards the revocation event to its own downstream peers. This fan-out propagation model ensures that compromised agents are excluded from the ecosystem within seconds rather than waiting for TTL expiry, which could be minutes or hours. To prevent replay attacks, each revocation event carries a monotonically increasing sequence number and a short validity window; resolvers reject revocation events with sequence numbers lower than the last processed event for a given agent identifier.

#### Threat Model and Resolver Security

The resolution infrastructure itself represents a high-value target, and AITRP incorporates specific defenses against attacks on the resolver layer.

**Cache poisoning.** All resolution responses are cryptographically signed by the authoritative zone resolver using its own key pair, analogous to DNSSEC response signing. Caching resolvers validate the authoritative signature before storing any record. A poisoned response that lacks a valid signature is discarded, and the caching resolver flags the upstream source for investigation. Response signatures cover the full record payload including the trust chain, preventing partial record substitution.

**Zone authority compromise.** If an authoritative zone resolver's signing key is compromised, the parent authority in the hierarchy can issue an emergency revocation for the zone's signing key, which propagates through the same revocation mechanism used for agent identities. Additionally, each zone's signing key is cross-signed by at least one peer zone authority, creating a secondary validation path. Resolvers that detect a mismatch between the zone signature and the cross-signature quarantine all records from the affected zone and escalate to the root authority.

**Denial of service against resolution queries.** The hierarchical caching architecture inherently mitigates denial of service by distributing query load across caching resolvers. For targeted attacks against authoritative resolvers, AITRP supports anycast deployment of zone resolvers (similar to how root DNS servers operate) and rate limiting with priority queuing that favors resolution queries from authenticated agents with valid identity records over anonymous queries.

**Record tampering in transit.** All resolver-to-resolver communication uses mutual TLS with certificate pinning. Identity records are independently verifiable because they carry the issuing authority's signature; even if an intermediary resolver is compromised and attempts to serve a modified record, the requesting agent's trust chain validation will detect the invalid signature and reject the record.
